name: Fire in the City
description: The capital of Berland looks like a rectangle of size n × m of the square blocks of same size. Fire! It is known that k + 1 blocks got caught on fire ( k + 1 ≤ n · m ). Those blocks are centers of ignition. Moreover positions of k of these centers are known and one of these stays unknown. All k + 1 positions are distinct. The fire goes the following way: during the zero minute of fire only these k + 1 centers of ignition are burning. Every next minute the fire goes to all neighbouring blocks to the one which is burning. You can consider blocks to burn for so long that this time exceeds the time taken in the problem. The neighbouring blocks are those that touch the current block by a side or by a corner. Berland Fire Deparment wants to estimate the minimal time it takes the fire to lighten up the whole city. Remember that the positions of k blocks (centers of ignition) are known and ( k + 1 )-th can be positioned in any other block. Help Berland Fire Department to estimate the minimal time it takes the fire to lighten up the whole city.
input_specification: The first line contains three integers n , m and k ( 1 ≤ n , m ≤ 10 9 , 1 ≤ k ≤ 500 ). Each of the next k lines contain two integers x i and y i ( 1 ≤ x i ≤ n , 1 ≤ y i ≤ m ) — coordinates of the i -th center of ignition. It is guaranteed that the locations of all centers of ignition are distinct.
output_specification: Print the minimal time it takes the fire to lighten up the whole city (in minutes).
approach_summary: Build a Segment Tree over the array. Implement point update and associative range query operations in O(log N) time per query.

topic_editorial.title: Editorial: 845E — Fire in the City [57. Segment Tree (Point Update Range Query)]
topic_editorial.summary: Range queries and updates via Segment Tree.
topic_editorial.key_invariant: The query operation is associative (e.g., sum, min, max, gcd). Any contiguous range $[L, R]$ can be decomposed into at most $O(\log N)$ canonical dyadic intervals represented by nodes in a binary tree.
topic_editorial.solution_walkthrough:
### Step 1: Tree Construction
We build a binary segment tree over array $A[1..N]$.
Each node covers a segment $[L, R]$. If $L = R$, the node stores $A[L]$. Otherwise:
$$\text{node.val} = \text{combine}(\text{left\_child.val}, \text{right\_child.val})$$

### Step 2: Point / Range Updates
To update position $pos$ with value $val$:
- Traverse down to the leaf node $[pos, pos]$.
- Update leaf value.
- Recompute ancestor values on the way back up in $O(\log N)$ time.

### Step 3: Range Query Processing
To query the associative aggregate on range $[qL, qR]$:
- If current segment $[L, R]$ is completely within $[qL, qR]$, return node value.
- If disjoint, return identity element.
- Otherwise, split and return $\text{combine}(\text{query}(left), \text{query}(right))$.
topic_editorial.complexity_analysis:
- **Time Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}((N + Q) \log N)$
  Building the segment tree takes $\mathcal{O}(N)$. Each point/range query and update traverses at most $4 \log N$ tree nodes, requiring $\mathcal{O}(\log N)$ time per query.
- **Space Complexity:** $\mathcal{O}(N)$
  A standard binary segment tree requires at most $4N$ nodes to represent elements up to index $N$.
